name: Neuramis

card.summary: A Korean hyaluronic acid filler range from Medytox used to smooth lines and add volume to lips, cheeks and the mid-face.
card.aka: Medytox HA filler; Neuramis Deep, Volume, Light
card.note: Injected by clinicians; availability varies by country and the line is not FDA-approved in the US.[1]

quick.overview:
Neuramis is a line of cross-linked hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal fillers made by South Korean company Medytox. Variants are designed for different depths, from superficial lines to nasolabial folds, lips and volume in areas such as the cheeks and chin.[1]

For appearance, HA fillers add volume and smooth folds, which can restore mid-face fullness or refine contour. Randomized trials in Korea compared Neuramis products with Restylane, Perlane and Juvederm Voluma and reported similar results.[2][3][4][5]
quick.how: A trained clinician injects the gel, and many variants include lidocaine for comfort.[4] Results are described as lasting months rather than permanently; in one mid-face study about 73 to 74 percent of subjects still responded at 104 weeks.[3] Hyaluronidase can dissolve HA fillers.[6]
quick.risks: Reported effects of HA fillers include swelling, bruising, redness and in rare cases vascular occlusion or granulomas.[6] In a network meta-analysis of cheek fillers, Giselleligne showed fewer adverse events than Neuramis Lidocaine, while efficacy scores did not differ significantly.[7] Neuramis has not received US FDA approval.[1]

lead: Neuramis is a range of cross-linked hyaluronic acid dermal fillers manufactured by Medytox, a South Korean biopharmaceutical company. Its variants include Light (superficial wrinkles and skin hydration), standard and Deep (medium to deep wrinkles, nasolabial folds, lips) and Volume (cheeks, chin and contouring), many with lidocaine for comfort.[1]

People use HA fillers to soften folds, add lip fullness and restore or build mid-face volume. Hyaluronic acid binds water and swells into a gel, and the effect of fillers generally lasts about 6 to 12 months; wrinkle fillers in general are temporary because the body gradually metabolizes them.[6][10]

Published research on Neuramis consists mostly of Korean randomized, split-face comparisons, several of them registered on ClinicalTrials.gov between 2012 and 2018. A 2015 phase III trial found Neuramis Deep non-inferior to Restylane for nasolabial folds,[5] a 2016 trial found Neuramis Deep Lidocaine scored somewhat better than Perlane-L on wrinkle and global improvement scales at 24 weeks,[4] and a mid-face trial found Neuramis Volume Lidocaine non-inferior to Juvederm Voluma.[2]

Neuramis carries the CE mark in Europe and is registered in South Korea, but the finished products are not FDA-approved or authorized for cosmetic sale in the United States, where only a small number of fillers are approved as medical devices.[1][10]

chain: Clinician injects HA gel into folds, lips or cheeks
Gel binds water and adds volume
Smoother folds and fuller mid-face for months
angle.text: Neuramis fillers add volume where the face has lost or lacks it. Different variants are formulated for fine lines, nasolabial folds, lips and cheeks, so a clinician can match gel firmness to the area being shaped.

paras: Neuramis is made by Medytox Inc., a company headquartered in Cheongju, South Korea, which also manufactures botulinum toxin products.[1] According to the Grokipedia entry, which draws on manufacturer material, the HA is produced by microbial fermentation rather than from animal tissue, is cross-linked in a two-step process the company calls SHAPE, and is supplied at 20 mg/mL in 1 mL syringes; lidocaine variants contain 0.3 percent lidocaine.[1] These figures are manufacturer-reported.

Most HA fillers are cross-linked with BDDE (1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether) so that the gel resists breakdown. Residual cross-linker is a topic of ongoing review in the wider filler literature, and Neuramis marketing material states that residual levels are minimal or non-detectable.[1][10]

Light Lidocaine is positioned for superficial lines and skin hydration. The standard Lidocaine product targets medium-depth wrinkles. Deep and Deep Lidocaine target medium-to-deep folds such as the nasolabial folds and lip augmentation. Volume Lidocaine, the most highly cross-linked variant, is designed for cheeks, chin, temples and jawline contouring.[1] The company's stated duration ranges from about 4 to 12 months depending on the variant.[1]

Neuramis variants target different depths: lighter products for fine lines and hydration, mid-depth products for wrinkles and lips, and Volume for cheek and chin contouring.[1] Clinics offering Korean aesthetic procedures commonly use such fillers for mid-face restoration and nasolabial folds.

In looksmaxxing and aesthetics discussion more broadly, HA fillers are described as a non-surgical way to add cheek projection, define the chin or jaw, soften under-eye or nasolabial hollows and shape lips. Proponents value that results appear immediately and can be adjusted or, with hyaluronidase, reversed.[6][9]

Per the Grokipedia entry, Neuramis Deep received the CE mark in 2011, with South Korean (MFDS) approval for Deep in 2013, Deep Lidocaine in 2014 and the Lidocaine series in 2015.[1] The HA raw material is registered in the FDA Drug Master File and certified by the EDQM, which is not the same as approval of the finished filler.[1] The entry gives inconsistent figures for market reach, citing registration in 36 countries in one place and marketing in about 60 countries in another.[1]

Wikipedia notes that in the United States fillers are regulated by the FDA as medical devices and only a handful are approved, while the EU lists more than 140 fillers, where a CE mark requires adherence to production standards rather than proof of medical efficacy.[10] Who may inject fillers is debated between physicians and licensed aestheticians.[10]

A phase III study of Neuramis in nasolabial folds was registered as NCT01585220 (started February 2012, 69 participants), and an NCT02751034 phase III study of Neuramis Deep Lidocaine began in June 2013 with 60 participants.[11][12] Later registrations include Neuramis Volume Lidocaine in mid-face volume loss (NCT02721368, 88 participants, from 2016; NCT03754413, 236 participants, from 2018) and Neuramis Deep Lidocaine against YVOIRE Volume Plus for nasolabial folds (NCT03753152, 370 participants, from 2018).[13][14][15]

A 67-person phase III trial found Neuramis Deep not inferior to Restylane, with no significant difference in safety.[5] The Grokipedia summary reports a mean Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale improvement of 0.50 at 24 weeks and local adverse events in 84 percent of Neuramis subjects (bruising about 70 percent, swelling about 62 percent), comparable to the control; one serious event was judged unrelated.[1] A 58-patient trial found WSRS improvement of 1.64 for Neuramis Deep Lidocaine versus 1.45 for Perlane-L at week 24.[4]

In a split-face trial of 88 Korean adults with age-related mid-face volume deficit, Neuramis Volume Lidocaine and Juvederm Voluma with Lidocaine each produced a 96.39% response rate at 24 weeks, meeting non-inferiority.[2] A 2-year extension followed 69 participants: responder rates were 73.91% for Neuramis and 72.46% for Juvederm at week 104, with no serious adverse events.[3]

A 2024 network meta-analysis of six randomized trials (579 patients) reported Giselleligne had fewer adverse events than VYC-20, ART-Filler and Neuramis Lidocaine, with no significant Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale differences among fillers.[7] In a mini-pig study comparing 14 HA fillers, Neuramis products tended to show lower inflammatory cell infiltration than Juvederm and Restylane products.[8]

Hyaluronidase breaks down hyaluronan and is the standard way to dissolve HA fillers, including after lip augmentation or when a complication occurs.[9] Recombinant human hyaluronidase (Hylenex) was approved in the US in December 2005.[9] Grokipedia reports that dissolution of Neuramis with hyaluronidase rests on animal-model data showing near-complete elimination of the filler within two weeks.[1]

Common reactions to HA fillers are bruising, redness, pain and itching; less often infection or allergic reactions that cause lumps or scarring.[10] The most serious complications are embolization into the arteries supplying the eye or skin, which can cause permanent vision loss or delayed skin necrosis; Wikipedia notes embolic events are more frequent with autologous fat, followed by HA.[10] Nerve or microvessel injury and granulomatous reactions are also reported.[6]

Wikipedia cites a 2015 study linking BDDE exposure to allergic reactions in 34.3 percent of a 452-patient cohort and a 2024 review questioning long-term BDDE safety.[10] Medical regulators and professional bodies generally advise that fillers be injected by trained clinicians.

Neuramis is one of several Korean HA filler brands in a market that also includes Restylane, Juvederm and Belotero. Medytox has been in the news chiefly for its botulinum toxin business, whereas Neuramis is the company's filler line.[1] Wikipedia describes fillers as having grown in popularity through wide application from the 1980s.[10]

timeline.event: Neuramis Deep receives the CE mark.[1]
Phase III trial of Neuramis in nasolabial folds begins (NCT01585220).[11]
Neuramis Deep approved in South Korea; Deep Lidocaine phase III trial starts.[1][12]
Phase III trial comparing Neuramis Deep and Restylane published; Lidocaine series approved in Korea.[1][5]
Trial of Neuramis Deep Lidocaine versus Perlane-L published; Volume Lidocaine mid-face trial begins.[4][13]
Larger Volume Lidocaine and Deep Lidocaine versus YVOIRE Volume Plus trials begin.[14][15]
Mid-face RCT of Neuramis Volume Lidocaine versus Juvederm Voluma published.[2]
2-year extension study and 14-filler mini-pig comparison published.[3][8]
Network meta-analysis of cheek fillers includes Neuramis Lidocaine.[7]

lore.intro: Neuramis is discussed less in forums than in clinic and distributor material; the points below reflect how HA fillers as a class are described by proponents and by researchers.[1][10]

claims.claim: Fillers give an immediate, adjustable change to cheeks, chin and lips
claims.believers: Proponents say HA gel adds visible volume right after treatment and can be topped up or dissolved if the result is not wanted.[1][9]
claims.experts: Trials of Neuramis Volume Lidocaine reported 96.39% response at 24 weeks on a mid-face volume scale.[2]

claims.claim: Korean-made fillers match the big Western brands
claims.believers: Manufacturer and clinic material says Neuramis performs comparably to Restylane, Perlane and Juvederm Voluma.[1]
claims.experts: Korean randomized trials reported non-inferiority or small advantages at 24 weeks, though many were sponsored or regional studies in Asian participants.[2][4][5]

claims.claim: Results last a year or more
claims.believers: Product descriptions cite up to 12 months, and a 2-year extension reported about 73 percent responders at 104 weeks.[1][3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says wrinkle fillers generally last about six months and that activity in the area can shorten duration.[10]

claims.claim: Fillers can be undone if unhappy
claims.believers: Clinics point to hyaluronidase as a safety net that dissolves HA gel.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes hyaluronidase as the main treatment for dissolving HA filler; Neuramis-specific data cited by Grokipedia are from animal models.[1][9]

claims.claim: Some fillers are gentler on tissue than others
claims.believers: Marketing for Neuramis stresses purification and low residual cross-linker.[1]
claims.experts: A mini-pig study found lower inflammatory infiltration for Neuramis products than some comparators, while a meta-analysis found Giselleligne had fewer adverse events than Neuramis Lidocaine.[7][8]

claims.claim: Filler complications are rare enough to be minor
claims.believers: Trial reports describe mostly mild, temporary injection-site reactions.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes vascular embolization can cause permanent blindness or skin necrosis, and regulators treat fillers as medical devices.[10]
